name: Emeka Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a filling and packing line at a food plant on the ring road, where we make jarred sauces, the tomato and basil one is the big seller. The line fills the jars, caps them, labels them, and two robot arms stack them onto pallets. My job is keeping all of that running: clearing jams, changing labels, adjusting the fill heads and calling in maintenance when I can't sort it myself. The fun part is a fault I can fix in five minutes. The boring part is a twelve-hour shift where nothing goes wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said 'when I can't sort it myself'. How do you sort things out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, half the time I've got my phone out with an AI assistant, typing in the fault code from the screen and asking what it means. It reads the manual faster than I can and it's usually right, or at least points me the right way. I'm also doing an online course in PLC programming at night, that's the little computers that control the machines, because I want to be the one writing the logic, not just pressing reset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, fair enough, it's a useful tool and not much more. I'd keep posting the occasional tip about using AI for fault codes, because it really does help. I wouldn't gloat, I'd just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed. I like this stuff, and part of me was looking forward to things getting more interesting. If AI turns out to be a fancy manual reader, I'll be the guy on the sauce line who reads manuals slightly faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course anyway, because that's useful whatever happens. I'd keep about nine months of savings in the bank and keep putting a bit into my index fund every month. Then I'd apply for a controls technician role, probably within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored. Like a film with a big trailer and a dull ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings and an index fund at twenty-seven. How did that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum drilled it into me, and the shift pay here is good. I share a flat with my cousin Tunde, so rent is cheap. I put a fixed amount into the fund every payday and I don't look at it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about your workplace bother you, even with no change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay gap. The owners just opened a second plant and we got a two percent rise. I'd keep pushing for us to join the union properly, because a quiet AI future doesn't fix that.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, AI turned out to be a useful tool and not much more. I'd keep sharing tips about using it for fault codes and carry on.
S0.think: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was looking forward to work getting more interesting. I'd just be the guy on the sauce line who reads manuals slightly faster.
S0.do: Finishes his PLC programming course and applies for a controls technician job within a year. Keeps his savings steady, pays monthly into his index fund and pushes for the union.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored, with a touch of disappointment.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be a fancy manual reader, I'll be the guy on the sauce line who reads manuals slightly faster.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is the rare worker who'd be let down by AI being hype. He already uses AI daily and is studying to move up into controls. His progressive side shows in his frustration over pay rather than over technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get ahead of it, and I'd say it loudly to the younger guys on the line. Learn the systems, don't be scared of them. I'd also say the companies should share the gains, because the robots make money and the workers should see some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is good for me, at least for a while. The people who can talk to the machines will be needed, and I'm already halfway there. The danger is for the people who can't or won't switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course faster, maybe add a robotics certificate, and ask the plant to let me help set up any new kit. I'd suggest automating the label changes myself, because it's the most boring part of the job. And I'd start pushing for a training fund in the union deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. But I'd feel guilty about being excited when other people are scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd suggest automating part of your own job. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But if someone's going to automate the label changes, I'd rather it was me, so I understand it when it breaks at two in the morning. The person who installs it usually keeps a job looking after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta on the capper. She's forty-eight, brilliant at her job, and she refuses to use the touchscreen, she calls the night shift manager to do it. If it all goes digital, she's in trouble, and I'd try to show her the basics on my breaks.

S1.say: I'd tell the younger workers to get ahead of this and learn the systems instead of fearing them. I'd also say companies should share the gains with workers.
S1.think: I think this is good for me, at least for a while, because people who can talk to the machines will be needed. The danger is for the people who can't or won't switch.
S1.do: Speeds up his PLC course, adds a robotics certificate and volunteers to help set up new equipment. Proposes automating label changes himself and pushes for a union training fund.
S1.feel: Calm and somewhat excited, with guilt about feeling that way when others are scared.
S1.quote: if someone's going to automate the label changes, I'd rather it was me, so I understand it when it breaks at two in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: Emeka is ready to automate part of his own job, reasoning that whoever installs it keeps the job of maintaining it. His guilt about his own excitement is telling. He looks out for an older colleague who avoids screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be shared, full stop. If machines can do all the work, then the profits belong to everyone, through taxes, a basic income, shorter hours, whatever works. I'd be online arguing about it every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is where my plan stops working. If AI can do almost any job, it can write PLC logic too, probably better than me. I've spent two years learning to talk to the machines, and in this picture the machines don't need anyone to talk to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job as long as it lasted and save everything I could. I'd join a campaign for a basic income and vote for whoever backed it. And, I'll be honest, I'd move some savings into the companies building the robots, because if they're going to own everything, I want a slice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel I could do something, but for the first time I wouldn't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want the profits shared, but you'd buy shares in the robot companies. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't, really, and I know it. I'd vote to tax those companies hard and still own a bit of them, because I can't control the vote but I can control my savings. It's a hedge, not a belief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do with your evenings instead of the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still finish it, because two years of better pay is two years of saving. But I'd spend more time on organising, writing to politicians, that sort of thing. My cousin Tunde says I'd become unbearable at dinner.

S2.say: I'd say the gains have to be shared, full stop, through taxes, a basic income or shorter hours. I'd argue about it online every night.
S2.think: This is where my plan stops working. If AI can do almost any job, it can write PLC logic better than me, and everything I've been learning stops mattering.
S2.do: Keeps his job as long as it lasts and saves hard. Campaigns and votes for a basic income, and moves some savings into robotics companies as a hedge.
S2.feel: Anxious, still feeling capable but unsure for the first time what to do.
S2.quote: I've spent two years learning to talk to the machines, and in this picture the machines don't need anyone to talk to them.
S2.fieldNote: For Emeka, fast AGI breaks the logic of upskilling, which is what he was counting on. He openly admits the clash between buying robot shares and wanting those companies taxed. His strong savings keep him from panic, but he has no plan for a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to set up a fair system if we start now. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen: shared ownership, retraining money, a basic income ready before the robots, not after. I'd be one of the people organising a union drive at the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to make some money from the skills I have before they're worth nothing. Controls technicians would be in huge demand right up until AGI lands. I'd ride that wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course in the first year and move to a controls job at a bigger plant, probably for twenty percent more pay. I'd put the extra into savings and into the index fund. And I'd stay active with the union and the basic income campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel like I was surfing a wave and I could see the beach coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly, and time to think. Two years is a fire alarm. Five years is more like a notice from the landlord, you have time to pack properly. I'd end up with a much bigger cushion when it hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at year five, when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I'm not going to pretend I do. I'd have savings, some shares, and hopefully a government that's done something sensible. I'd try to find whatever humans are still wanted for, maybe teaching or looking after people.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to build a fair system if we start now: shared ownership, retraining money and a basic income ready before the robots. I'd help organise a union drive at the plant.
S3.think: Five years lets me cash in on my controls skills while they're in demand. I'd ride that wave and build up as much money as I can before it ends.
S3.do: Finishes his course in the first year and moves to a better-paid controls job at a bigger plant. Puts the extra pay into savings and his index fund while staying active in the union and basic income campaign.
S3.feel: Uneasy, enjoying the ride but able to see where it ends.
S3.quote: Two years is a fire alarm. Five years is more like a notice from the landlord, you have time to pack properly.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Emeka shifts from fighting to cashing in while still campaigning. His metaphor of the fire alarm versus a landlord's notice sums up the difference time makes. He is honest that he has no idea what he'd do once AGI actually arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be a crime. We should use it to change how work and money are shared. I'd be pushing for a shorter working week to start now, so people get used to having less work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd have a good career in controls for maybe seven or eight years, then I'd want to move into something people still want from a person, like teaching trades or community work. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move into a controls job and use AI tools every day to get better faster. Around year five I'd start a part-time teaching qualification. I'd keep saving and investing every month, and stay in the campaign for shared ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mild way. I'd mostly feel lucky to have the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching, if AI can teach too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it can, but I think people still want a person in the room, especially young people who are lost. I'd like to help kids from my estate, the ones who'd be growing up without the factory jobs we had. That feels worth doing even if a machine could do it cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you wait too long because ten years feels far off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. That's why I'd set dates, like a reminder on my phone: year five, start the teaching course. I'm good at planning, I'm just bad at stopping when the plan is going well.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and wasting it would be a crime. We should use it to change how work and money are shared, starting with a shorter working week now.
S4.think: Privately, ten years feels manageable: seven or eight years in controls, then a move into teaching trades or community work at around thirty-seven.
S4.do: Moves into a controls job in the first year and uses AI tools daily to build skills. Starts a part-time teaching qualification around year five while saving, investing and campaigning for shared ownership.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy, but mostly lucky to have the time.
S4.quote: I'm good at planning, I'm just bad at stopping when the plan is going well.
S4.fieldNote: Emeka's ten-year plan is the most detailed of his five, with dates and a second career. He wants to help young people from his estate, which links his politics to his plans. He's aware his weakness is getting comfortable when things are going well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where all my planning is useless. I'm the guy who always has a plan, and in that picture I'd just have a bank balance and an opinion. What would help is a basic income or a share of the profits ready to switch on, so people like me aren't relying on luck.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd still enjoy the robots. I would. That's the strange part, I'd be fighting for a fair share and still find the machines fascinating.

headlineQuote: I'm the guy who always has a plan, and in that picture I'd just have a bank balance and an opinion.
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old who runs a jarred-sauce filling line, uses AI daily to read fault codes and is studying PLC programming to move into controls work. He shares a flat with his cousin, saves steadily and invests in an index fund. He's calm and even excited in the plateau and steady disruption pictures, but fast AGI unsettles him because it makes his upskilling pointless. With five or ten years he plans to cash in on controls work and later teach, while campaigning for shared ownership and admitting he'd buy robot shares as a hedge.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because it's the only picture where all his planning becomes useless.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or a share of automation profits that's ready to switch on, so people aren't relying on luck.
